guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

The inner child often becomes loudest in the gap after one life has ended and before the next has formed: after a breakup, migration, illness, loss of faith, loss of a role, a child leaving home, or the decision to leave a family or community on different terms.

Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You do not have to accept its teachings about death or rebirth to use the ordinary-life insight: endings create a period with no familiar identity and no clear replacement.

Ask:

What has actually ended?

What am I still trying to make continue?

What is not known yet?

What does the child fear will happen in the gap?

What practical act or small ritual would mark the ending without pretending I know the next beginning?

Do not force a new identity because uncertainty feels unbearable. The adult can keep routines, protect the body, grieve what ended, and remain with the child while the next life takes shape.

Missing somebody does not have to become another problem to solve. Sometimes the ache itself can become a cue for love. Do not push the missing away. If love is accessible, let “I miss you” become “I love you,” or offer a simple loving-kindness wish: “May you be safe. May you be held in love.” You can picture the person or simply feel the direction of care. This practice is about what happens in you; it does not require believing the other person receives anything, and it does not replace grief, contact, boundaries, or practical action. If sending love makes you more compulsive, unreal, or unable to return to your life, make it simpler: “I miss you, and I care.” You can also notice the part of you that is still here and offer some of the same care inward.
note: Turn 65 (2026-10-17): the guide after Simple Practices, group le01 (When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun), for the dedup.
before: Forgiving yourself works the same way, and when it's hard, forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Once you've faced the responsibility, you're allowed to release it and stop holding yourself hostage. Some harms take years. Forgiving too soon is one trap, and living permanently inside resentment is the other. Now and then, come back to the question of how they became capable of it, without forcing anything, until the understanding is real enough to change how you feel.
